rules.title: Prohibition on coordinated pricing algorithms to set rents or manage occupancy (BMC ch. 13.63)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license or otherwise provide to Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels, and unlawful for a landlord to use one when setting rents or occupancy levels for Berkeley residential units. Each month of violation and each unit affected is a separate violation.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms (using nonpublic competitor data under 90 days old) for setting rents or occupancy levels
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley. A 'coordinated pricing algorithm' uses Competitor Data (nonpublic data on other properties, less than 90 days old) to recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination between a Berkeley landlord and its competitors, including through a third-party vendor.
rules.exemptions: Excludes (a) products that publish aggregated, anonymous rental data without recommending rents, fees or occupancy rates; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines; (c) products used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development. The chapter does not regulate the amount of rent a landlord may charge.
rules.interaction: Local ordinance. This document does not address state or other preemption.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.conflict_note: Open question: two published effective dates exist for this ban (1 March 2026 in the ordinance text per the brief; January 2026 per an August 2026 law-firm alert). Neither effective date is stated in this capture.
rules.notes: This document states no effective date, so effective_date is null. It records only that the Council passed the ordinance to print on November 18, 2025 (first reading). The final adoption date is not stated, so adoption_date is null. Status is in_force on the assumption that the ordinance took effect before the 2026-10-01 query date under either published date. Civil remedies of up to $1,000 per violation are omitted from key_value. Effective date from D002: "13.63 (effective January 2026) Prohibits coordinated pricing algorithms;"

rules.key_value: Nonpayment eviction only if rent debt is at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent (Oakland-Fremont metro) for an equivalent-size unit
rules.coverage_conditions: Units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance, including government-owned or -subsidized units now required to register as fully or partially covered. | [D009] Fully covered: most units in multifamily properties built before 1980; single family homes with tenancies that began before 1996; rooming houses. rules.exemptions: Exempt units are outside the ordinance. rules.title: Cartwright Act ban on common pricing algorithms (AB 325)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination or conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use or distribute one while coercing another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term.
rules.key_value: Ban on using or distributing a common pricing algorithm in a combination/conspiracy to restrain trade, or while coercing adoption of its recommended prices
rules.coverage_conditions: General antitrust law, not rental-specific. A 'common pricing algorithm' is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. | [D093] Applies to any person using or distributing a methodology (including software) used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. It is not limited to housing; it covers rental pricing as a product or service. | [D028] A pricing algorithm is 'common' if it has two or more users and uses competitor data to recommend or influence prices or other commercial terms. Applies to any industry, not only rental housing. | [M_CA-ALG-01_BPC_16729_justia] Applies to any 'person' (as defined in Bus. & Prof. Code § 16702), excluding end consumers. 'Common pricing algorithm' means any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
rules.exemptions: 'Person' does not include the end consumer of a product or service. | [D093] Does not apply to end consumers of a product or service. | [D028] Single-firm or proprietary algorithms that use only the business's own data are not covered. | [M_CA-ALG-01_BPC_16729_justia] End consumers of a product or service are not covered 'persons'.
rules.interaction: Statewide; Section 16729(c) says it does not impair or limit the applicability of antitrust laws. Does not address local ordinances in this text.

rules.title: Rental broker fees payable only by the party who engaged the broker
rules.requirement: Only a licensed broker or salesperson may find dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. Any fee must be paid only by the lessor or tenant who originally engaged and contracted with the broker or salesperson.
rules.key_value: Broker fee payable only by the party (landlord or tenant) who hired the broker
rules.coverage_conditions: Persons engaged in finding rental dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee; the broker or salesperson must be licensed under c.112 § 87PP.
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.
rules.notes: Effective date taken from the page's update note: amended by St. 2025, c. 9, § 43, effective August 1, 2025. A broker-fee rule is not strictly an application or screening fee; it is filed here as the nearest category (fees charged to rental applicants). The document is an unofficial text of the statute.

rules.title: Broker fee payable only by the party who engaged the broker
rules.requirement: A licensed broker or salesperson may contract with either the prospective tenant or the landlord, not both, and any fee must be paid only by the party who originally engaged the broker. A landlord's broker therefore cannot charge the tenant a fee.
rules.key_value: Broker fee payable only by the party (lessor or tenant) who engaged the broker
rules.coverage_conditions: Licensed brokers and salespersons finding rental residential real property; persons finding dwellings for prospective tenants for a fee must be licensed.
rules.citation: M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD½, as amended by St. 2025, c. 9, § 43
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.
rules.notes: Broker (finder's) fee rule, not strictly a screening fee. Closest fit among the allowed categories is fees charged to rental applicants. Effective date from the header 'Text of section as amended by 2025, 9, Sec. 43 effective August 1, 2025'. The earlier text only required a broker license.

rules.title: No application fees by landlords (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B)
rules.requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a lessor may require payment only of first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit and a lock fee; application, pet, cleaning and amenity fees are forbidden. rules.key_value: Landlords may not charge application fees; only first, last, security deposit and locks may be collected
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to lessors (landlords) before the start of a tenancy; a landlord who is also a broker is likely treated as a landlord first (not settled by appellate case law).
rules.exemptions: Licensed brokers may charge fees under 254 CMR 7 if they follow the board of registration's regulations, including a separate bona fide brokerage operation.

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21 (statewide rent increase limit) barred from ballot
rules.requirement: The petition would have repealed c. 40P and capped annual rent increases for covered dwelling units. The SJC held it relates to religion because of its exemption for religious facilities, so art. 48 bars it from the November 2026 ballot.
rules.key_value: Would have capped annual rent increases at the lower of CPI increase or 5%; not law
rules.coverage_conditions: Would have covered all dwelling units leased for residential, but not commercial, use.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units; units with rents regulated by a public authority; units rented primarily to transient guests for under 14 consecutive days; units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or non-profit purposes; units whose first residential certificate of occupancy is less than 10 years old (for 10 years from issuance).
rules.interaction: Would have ended the statewide prohibition on rent control in G. L. c. 40P; that prohibition remains in force.
rules.citation: Initiative Petition 25-21; Mass. Const. Amend. art. 48, The Initiative, II, § 2; Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893 (2026)

The petition proposes a

limit on annual rent increases for residential dwelling units

"facilities operated solely for . . . religious . . . purposes."

rules.title: No local rent control permitted (state bar), G.L. c. 40P, § 4
rules.requirement: Cities and towns may not enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. The only exception is for a municipality that accepts chapter 40P and adopts regulation that is voluntary after six months, excludes owners of fewer than ten rental units and units with fair market rent above $400, and compensates owners from general funds.
rules.key_value: No rent cap: state law bars local rent control
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to every Massachusetts city and town. The narrow exception applies only to a municipality that accepts chapter 40P, and then only to rental units owned by a person or entity owning ten or more rental units and with fair market rent of $400 or less.
rules.exemptions: Exception for municipalities accepting the chapter: compliance is voluntary after six months from initial adoption. The regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation. The municipality must compensate owners for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent from general funds.
rules.interaction: Preempts local rent control in MA municipalities, including Boston and Cambridge, so no local rent-increase cap applies to them under this statute.
rules.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:
rules.notes: The official code text states no effective date, so effective_date is null. The section is treated as in force because it is in the current official General Laws. The exception requires a municipality to accept chapter 40P; this document does not say whether any municipality has done so.

rules.title: No rent control permitted (state bar, G. L. c. 40P)
rules.requirement: Massachusetts law broadly prohibits any regulatory scheme based on or implementing rent control, including any regulation requiring below-market residential rents.

rules.interaction: Bars local rent control ordinances. Initiative Petition 25-21 would have struck out c. 40P, but the SJC held it cannot be placed on the November 2026 ballot, so the ban remains.

rules.notes: Secondary description of c. 40P in a court opinion; the statute's enactment/effective date is not stated in this document, so effective_date is null.

rules.title: CORI access limits for evaluating rental housing applicants
rules.requirement: A landlord may obtain CORI to evaluate rental applicants only if the applicant has signed an acknowledgement form, and the information is limited to felony convictions (10 years), misdemeanor convictions (5 years) and pending charges. A landlord holding an applicant's criminal history must give the applicant a copy before questioning them about it and if an adverse housing decision is made on that basis.
rules.key_value: Lookback limits: felonies 10 years, misdemeanors 5 years from disposition (incl. end of incarceration/custody), plus pending charges
rules.coverage_conditions: Requestors evaluating applicants for rental or lease of housing under § 172(a)(3)(ii); requestor must certify under penalty of perjury and keep the subject's signed acknowledgement form for 1 year. | [M_MA-SCRN-02_803_CMR_5] Applies to landlords, real estate agents, public housing authorities and property management companies that request CORI to screen applicants to rent or lease housing, including market-rate and subsidized housing. | [M_MA-SCRN-02_MGL_c6_s172_findlaw] Applies to a requestor evaluating applicants for rental or lease of housing, under subsection (a)(3). Requestor must certify purpose and have the applicant's signed acknowledgement form, and must verify the applicant's identity.
rules.exemptions: Under § 172(b), convictions for murder, voluntary and involuntary manslaughter, and sex offenses punishable by state prison remain available permanently unless sealed. Prior convictions remain available as long as the last conviction is available. Housing authorities under c. 121B may obtain conviction and pending CORI for their own applications (§ 172(a)(7)). | [M_MA-SCRN-02_803_CMR_5] Standard access CORI may not be used to screen other household members, but open access CORI may be requested for individuals other than the applicant (5.04(3)-(4)). Landlords may still make an adverse decision based on an applicant's refusal to consent to a lawful CORI request (5.06(3)). | [M_MA-SCRN-02_MGL_c6_s172_findlaw] Under subsection (b), murder, voluntary and involuntary manslaughter, and state-prison-punishable sex offenses remain available permanently unless sealed. Prior convictions stay available for as long as the subject's last available conviction record is available. Housing authorities have separate access under (a)(7).
rules.quoted_span: Criminal offender record information made available under this section shall be limited to the following: (i) felony convictions or findings of not guilty by reason of insanity for 10 years following the disposition thereof, including termination of any period of incarceration or custody, (ii) misdemeanor convictions for 5 years following the disposition thereof, including termination of any period of incarceration or custody, and (iii) pending criminal charges, which shall include cases that have been continued without a finding until such time as the case is dismissed pursuant to section 18 of chapter 278

The duty to provide the criminal history to the applicant before questioning and before an adverse decision, and the ban on requesting CORI copies except as authorized (§ 172(d)), are folded into the requirement. The lookback limits apply to CORI obtained from the state database.

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit limits and handling (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B)
rules.requirement: At or before the start of a tenancy a landlord may collect only first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock. The deposit must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, with 5% annual interest (or the lesser amount the bank paid) paid to the tenant. It must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends, less itemized, sworn deductions for allowed items.
rules.key_value: Security deposit capped at 1 month's rent (plus first month, last month and lock/key cost); return within 30 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential leases and tenancies-at-will. The statute is not applicable to rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes.
rules.exemptions: Subsection (9): does not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which is for a vacation or recreational purpose.
rules.interaction: Statewide statute. Lease provisions that conflict with it, and tenant waivers, are void as against public policy.
rules.quoted_span: (b) At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following: (i) rent for the first full month of occupancy;  and, (ii) rent for the last full month of occupancy calculated at the same rate as the first month;  and, (iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);

The text was amended by 2025, c. 9, §§ 54-55, effective 2025-08-01 (adds 'agent of the lessor' and lets the executive office of housing and livable communities authorize an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, capped at 1 month's rent in total). That amendment did not change the cap itself. Procedural duties (receipts, condition statement, records, transfer to successor, treble damages) are folded into this record.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Makes it unlawful, and a violation of the NJ Antitrust Act, for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to facilitate rent-restricting agreements, and for anyone to perform a coordinating function or engage in parallel pricing coordination.
rules.key_value: Ban on algorithmic rent-setting coordination (use of coordinators / algorithmic devices performing a coordinating function)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental property owners (anyone owning one or more rental residential dwelling units) and coordinators operating algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function. Residential dwelling unit excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. | [D060] Residential rental property owners, property managers, and software providers/"coordinators" using algorithmic revenue management software or devices that use nonpublic, competitively sensitive information from multiple residential rental property owners.
rules.exemptions: Excludes spreadsheets operating without AI and requiring human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data. Also excludes research/statistical/testing use of information not used to set rents, free public rent estimates, equal-terms real estate brokerage databases that do not set or recommend rents, and government affordability controls. | [D060] Does not prohibit spreadsheets requiring human analysis, publicly available rent estimation tools, traditional real estate listing databases, and government-administered affordable housing programs.
rules.interaction: Section 6(b) prohibits municipalities from enacting ordinances that conflict with this act, except ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law. This may preempt local algorithmic-rent ordinances such as those of Jersey City and Hoboken once effective. The act is in addition to the NJ Antitrust Act.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful and a violation of the “New Jersey Antitrust Act,” P.L.1970, c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.) for: a. a rental property owner, or any agent, representative, or subcontractor thereof, to receive, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange any form of consideration in return for the use of, the services of a coordinator; b. a coordinator to facilitate a tacit or express agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition with respect to residential dwelling units, including by performing a coordinating function;
rules.conflict_note: Possible preemption of the Jersey City and Hoboken algorithmic-rent ordinances: section 6(b) bars municipal ordinances that conflict with the act. This document does not name those ordinances or resolve whether they conflict.
rules.notes: Section 9: takes effect on the first day of the twelfth month next following enactment. Enacted (approved) July 20, 2026, so the twelfth month following is July 2027, giving 2027-07-01. Not yet effective as of the 2026-10-01 query date. Text is the first reprint (A3497 1R ACS).

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap (P.L. 2025, c.405)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50. Violators face civil penalties and must refund the amount wrongfully charged to the applicant.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum, adjusted annually for CPI increases (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island CPI-U)
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property leased or subleased for dwelling purposes; applies to landlords and their agents.
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent; New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees, unless the licensee is the landlord of the property.
rules.interaction: State-wide cap with no stated preemption of local rules; local ordinances are not addressed in this document.
rules.quoted_span:
shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

Enactment (approval) was January 20, 2026, so the fourth month after is May, giving 2026-05-01. This is in force as of the 2026-10-01 query date. Penalties: up to $500 first offense, $750 second, $1,000 subsequent. The CPI adjustment begins January 1 of the year after enactment (2027), applies only if CPI change is greater than zero, and the Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the adjusted limit annually.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act (good cause required)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict or refuse to renew a lease, written or oral, without good cause under the Anti-Eviction Act. Possession may be recovered only through consent or court process, and a Notice to Quit is required for all good-cause evictions except nonpayment of rent.
rules.key_value: Good cause required to evict or fail to renew a residential lease
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and mobile home park land, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 to -84). | [D067] Rental dwelling units generally; tenants of public housing, rooming/boarding houses and senior/disabled protected tenancies have additional rules. Notice to Quit periods vary by cause (3 days to 3 years). | [D062] Houses, buildings, mobile homes or land in mobile home parks, or tenements leased for residential purposes.
rules.exemptions: May not apply to owner-occupied premises with two (2) or fewer rental units; does not apply to hotel or motel guests or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal tenants (except continual-residence occupants with no alternate residence); does not apply to a unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it. | [D067] Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings fall under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2, which allows a narrower list of grounds (holdover after lease expiry, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, willful damage, rule or lease violations). | [D062] Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units; hotels, motels or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal tenants; units held in trust for, or permanently occupied by, an immediate family member with a developmental disability.
rules.interaction: Statewide rule; applies regardless of local rent control. Self-help evictions and lockouts are illegal.
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
rules.notes: Effective date not stated in this document. Relocation-assistance duties are not addressed in this part of the guide. Summary of the statute found in the official DCA guide.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act: good cause required for lease non-renewal
rules.requirement: Landlords of covered residential rentals may not refuse to renew a written or oral lease unless they have good cause under the Anti-Eviction Act. The good causes are listed in the guide's Eviction section (not in this part).
rules.key_value: Good cause required to refuse renewal or evict; a lease term ending is not itself a ground
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties generally.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (which have a separate section), motels or hotels, and transient or seasonal units.
rules.quoted_span: No landlord of residential rental properties except t hose in owner occupied two or three family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient, or seasonal units may fail to renew any lease, regardless of whether it is written or oral unless they have good cause not to renew the lease.
rules.notes: Only the non-renewal summary appears in this part; the list of causes and any relocation-assistance duties are in later parts of the guide. The guide cites the statute as 'N.J.S.A. 2A:18:61.3'. No effective date is stated in this document.

rules.title: No statewide rent control (municipal option); rent increase notice and unconscionability standard
rules.requirement: New Jersey sets no statewide cap on rents, and municipalities may adopt their own rent control or leveling ordinances. A landlord may raise rent only by properly terminating the lease and offering a new one, and the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any local ordinance.
rules.key_value: No state rent cap; increases must not be unconscionable and must follow any municipal rent control ordinance
rules.coverage_conditions: Statewide; local rent control boards apply only where a municipality has adopted a rent control or leveling ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5); government-subsidized rents, HUD-owned/subsidized or HUD-insured developments, and NJHMFA-financed projects may also be exempt.
rules.interaction: State leaves rent regulation to municipalities; municipal ordinances (e.g. Jersey City, Hoboken, Newark) govern the allowable increases where they exist. State notice rules in the Anti-Eviction Act apply alongside local rules.
rules.quoted_span: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents.
rules.notes: Secondary summary by the state agency (DCA Truth in Renting guide). No effective date stated in this document. Increase procedure: written notice terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rent.

rules.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income / rent payment protection
rules.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent payment, so they cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment solely because of that income source.
rules.key_value: Ban on refusing tenants based on source of lawful income (including Section 8 vouchers)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, business or residential, including open land. | [D067] Applies to all landlord-tenant relationships, subject to the exceptions listed. | [D061] Applies to any person with the right to sell, rent, lease, assign or sublease real property, and to brokers, salespersons, agents and employees.
rules.exemptions: Rental of a single apartment in a two-family dwelling where the owner occupies the other unit; rental of rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling; religious-organization preference for persons of the same religion (sale/lease/rental); familial status rule does not apply to housing for older persons (N.J.S.A. 10:5-5mm). | [D067] Two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex (e.g. YMCA, age-restricted housing), as pertains to familial status. | [D061] Not stated in the source for the source-of-income provision. The sex-specific housing carve-out and the housing-for-older-persons exemption relate to other protected classes.
rules.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses.
rules.notes: Secondary summary brochure (rev. 06.18.15) of the LAD; the document states no effective date for the source-of-income provision, so effective_date is null. Complaints filed with the Division within 180 days; the Division does not handle ordinary landlord-tenant disputes such as evictions.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal record screening limits)
rules.requirement: A housing provider may not inquire about an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After the offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, and a withdrawal requires an individualized assessment and written notice.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; after offer, only convictions for listed serious offenses (no time limit) or indictable offenses within look-back periods of 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree) and 1 year (4th degree)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a 'rental dwelling unit', meaning a dwelling unit offered for rent by a housing provider for residential purposes, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: Housing providers may consider convictions for methamphetamine manufacture on the premises of federally assisted housing and lifetime sex offender registration status. Owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units are excluded.
rules.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
rules.notes: Effective date computed from section 14: the act takes effect on the first day of the seventh month next following enactment. Enactment was June 18, 2021 (Approved June 18, 2021), so the seventh month following is January 2022, giving 2022-01-01. Also folded in: written disclosure before accepting any application fee (s.4b), no evaluation of arrests without conviction, expunged or sealed records (s.5a), and a ban on requiring drug or alcohol tests (s.9). Enforcement is through the Division on Civil Rights, with penalties up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000.)

rules.title: NJ Security Deposit Law: cap of 1.5 months' rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit above one and one-half times one month's rent, and prepaid rent held as security (including last month's rent) counts toward that cap. Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account, with interest going to the tenant, and returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
rules.key_value: 1.5 months' rent maximum; annual increases limited to 10% of the current deposit
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes. | [D063] Real property used for dwelling purposes; applies to owners and lessees collecting security from a tenant.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (a tenant there may opt in 30 days after a written request to the landlord). The interest-account rules do not apply to seasonal rentals of not more than 125 consecutive days. Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, where the tenant has failed to provide 30 days written notice to the landlord invoking the provisions of the act.
rules.quoted_span: The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).
rules.notes: Secondary DCA guide summarizing the statute; no effective date is stated in this document. The guide also says a pet deposit combined with the regular deposit cannot exceed 1.5 months' rent, and that the landlord may require only the first month's rent in addition to the deposit (max 2.5 months' rent at lease inception). Return deadline: 30 days, with an itemized list of deductions sent by registered or certified mail.}},{ Supplementary provision folded in (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26: The security deposit act applies to all rental premises or units used for dwelling purposes. Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units are excluded unless the tenant gives the landlord 30 days written notice invoking the act.)

rules.title: Newark Rent Control: annual CPI-based rent increase cap
rules.requirement: At lease expiration (or termination of a periodic tenancy), a landlord may not request or receive an increase greater than the CPI-U percentage change (15 months prior to 3 months prior to the month of the increase), and never more than 4%. Written notice to the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer at least 30 days in advance is required. No increase is allowed if the unit is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not met registration requirements.
rules.key_value: CPI-U increase (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island), max 4% in any consecutive 12-month period
rules.coverage_conditions: All multiple dwellings as defined in § 19:2-2 are subject to rent control (§ 19:2-2.1). The cap applies per housing space in any consecutive twelve-month period, irrespective of tenant turnover, change of ownership or vacancy.
rules.exemptions: Exempt dwellings per § 19:2-2: public housing; hotel/motel space rented day-to-day to transients; commercial space; newly constructed multiple dwellings and vacant dwellings (§§ 19:2-18.1 and 19:2-18.2, not in this part); certain federal/state rehabilitated Section 8 units (rent capped at HUD fair market rent); units under a contract with a governmental agency that regulates rent.
rules.interaction: Board-approved surcharges (tax, major new improvement, hardship, utilities) are separate from this annual cap; the 25% ceiling in § 19:2-22 is not in this part. Local ordinance within NJ framework; no state-level conflict noted in this document.
rules.quoted_span: At the expiration of a lease or at the termination of the lease of a periodic tenant, no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.
rules.notes: Section history: Ord. 6 PSF-A(S), 9-5-2017; amended 9-18-2024 by Ord. No. 6PSF-I. Month of adoption; exact effective date not stated in source (NJ ordinances generally take effect after final passage and publication). Latest amendment date used; the document does not show whether the 2024 amendment changed the 4% cap or kept it as originally enacted in 2017. A 2026-06-17 ordinance (6PSF-C) amends only §§ 19:2-27 and 19:2-32 (habitability certificates), not this section. Document is part 1 of 3; § 19:2-18 and § 19:2-22 appear elsewhere. Supplementary provision folded in (Newark Rev. Gen. Ord. § 19:2-22: The Rent Control Board may not grant increases above 25% in any one year for any tenant. Increases under §§ 19:2-3, 19:2-7 and 19:2-8 within the 12 months before the effective date are added together when testing the 25% limit.) Supplementary provision folded in (Newark Rev. Gen. Ord. § 19:2-18.1: Rent control limits on periodic or regular increases do not apply to newly constructed multiple dwellings for a limited period. The period is the amortization period of the initial mortgage or 30 years after completion of construction, whichever is less.) Supplementary provision folded in (Newark Rev. Gen. Ord. § 19:2-18.4: A landlord who rehabilitates a vacant apartment by spending at least 12 months of actual monthly rent per unit may be granted a one-off increase of up to 10% in the actual monthly rent. Only one such increase is allowed per unit in any twelve-month period.) Supplementary provision folded in (Newark Rev. Gen. Ord. § 19:2-17.1: A landlord who shows heating and water expenses rose by more than 10% over the prior 12 months is granted a utilities surcharge. The surcharge is capped by building size as a share of the monthly rent roll.)

rules.title: Newark Ban the Box - Housing (criminal record check practices)
rules.requirement: A landlord or real estate broker may inquire into or consider an applicant's criminal history only after a formal application is submitted, and only after giving written notice. Look-back is limited to 8 years for indictable convictions and 5 years for disorderly persons or ordinance convictions, plus pending charges. Arrests without conviction, expunged or sealed records and juvenile adjudications may not be considered.
rules.key_value: No criminal history inquiry until after formal application; look-back 8 years (indictable) / 5 years (disorderly persons, municipal ordinance); murder, arson, registry sex offenses and terrorism convictions may be considered regardless of when they occurred
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental, lease or sublease of real property by landlords and real estate brokers; excludes (1) a single apartment in a two-family dwelling where the owner occupies the other unit and (2) a room or rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling.
rules.exemptions: Prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law requires or permits consideration of criminal history (limited to those offenses and periods), or to property designated for a government program that encourages housing for people with criminal histories. Exceptions are to be interpreted narrowly.
rules.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.
rules.notes: Month of adoption; exact effective date not stated in source (NJ ordinances generally take effect after final passage and publication). Adoption date 4-15-2015 is taken from the Ord. 6 PSF-B citation; the Editor's Note says the earlier Ord. 6 PSF-F (2012) was repealed by Ord. 6 PSF-B. Procedural duties folded in: 3 business days to submit evidence, adverse-action notice within 10 business days by registered mail, confidentiality, and a ban on advertisements referencing criminal history. Article 2 (City licensing) is outside scope.

rules.title: San Diego Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price Fixing (SDMC §98.1103)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license or provide an algorithmic device to a landlord, and unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.key_value: Ban on selling, licensing, or using algorithmic rent-setting devices (software using nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property in the City of San Diego; 'algorithmic device' means software that uses algorithms to calculate nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords to recommend rental rates or occupancy levels. | [D076] Residential rental property in the City of San Diego; applies to any person who sells or provides such devices to a landlord and to landlords who use them. 'Algorithmic device' means software that performs calculations on nonpublic competitor data to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels.
rules.exemptions: Excludes software that publishes reports from aggregated historical nonpublic data more than 90 days old or public information without recommending future rates; software used to set rents or income limits under affordable housing program guidelines; appraisal software that does not recommend rental rates during runtime. | [D076] Excludes (a) software that publishes reports from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from publicly available information, and does not recommend rates or occupancy levels for future leases or renewals; and (b) software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.interaction: No state or other-level interaction stated in this document. Remedies are cumulative with other law.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code § 98.1103 (Ord. O-21955 N.S.)
rules.quoted_span:
(b) It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or  
occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.notes: Added 5-22-2025 by O-21955 N.S.; effective 6-21-2025 per the document. Each month of violation per property is a separate violation; tenants may seek injunctive relief, damages or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation (§98.1104). Proposal (S.D. Mun. Code § 98.1103 (proposed; Ord. O-2025-107), D076) adopted as San Diego Municipal Code § 98.1103 (Ord. O-21955 N.S.).

rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections (just cause for termination of tenancy)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a covered tenancy without at-fault or no-fault just cause. For no-fault terminations the landlord must give relocation assistance, either as a direct payment within 15 days of the notice or as a rent waiver, and must notify the Housing Commission. Buyout agreements must follow written disclosure rules and may not be for less than the relocation amount.
rules.key_value: Just cause required; no-fault relocation assistance = 2 months' actual rent (3 months if tenant is a senior 62+ or disabled)
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property with a tenancy of more than 30 days. Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years is exempt (unless a mobilehome). Separately alienable property is exempt only if the landlord is not a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with a corporate member, or a mobilehome park management, and the tenant received the required written exemption notice. | [D077] Applies only to a 'Tenancy' (right to occupy more than 30 days; excludes fixed-term leases of 3 months or less). Excluded: housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome).
rules.exemptions: Includes transient/tourist hotels and short-term occupancy; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (but not Section 8); mobilehomes under the Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospitals, religious, care and transitional facilities; dormitories; shared-facility rentals with the landlord; owner-occupied single-family residences (up to two bedrooms or ADUs) and owner-occupied duplexes; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years; and qualifying separately alienable property with written notice. See § 98.0703. | [D077] Transient/tourist hotels; stays of 30 consecutive days or less; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (not applicable to Section 8 voucher tenants); mobilehomes subject to the MRL; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care or licensed elder care and nonprofit transitional housing; school-owned dormitories; shared bath/kitchen with owner; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than two units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplex; separately alienable units (e.g., condo) not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, with written exemption notice.
rules.interaction: Consistent with and additional to California Civil Code § 1946.2; the rights are in addition to any state or federal rights. Relocation assistance is credited against any other relocation assistance required by federal, state or other local law and is in addition to return of the security deposit.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.
rules.notes: Added 5-25-2023 by O-21647 N.S.; effective 6-24-2023. Amended 2-27-2024 by O-21769 N.S., effective 3-28-2024 (§§ 98.0702, 98.0704, 98.0709, 98.0710 added or amended). The amendment text does not show a change to the headline relocation figures, so the original effective date is used. Relocation amounts are in § 98.0706(c). At-fault grounds are in § 98.0704(a) and no-fault grounds in § 98.0704(b).

rules.title: San Diego Prohibition of Discrimination Based on a Tenant's Source of Income
rules.requirement: Landlords may not refuse to enter into or renew a tenancy, terminate a tenancy, or apply income standards that ignore a tenant's entire source of income, including rental assistance and vouchers, based on source of income. Income standards must account for aggregate income of co-tenants and cosigners on the same basis as married persons.
rules.key_value: Ban on source-of-income discrimination (includes federal, state, local or nonprofit rental assistance and subsidies)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental-units and tenancies in the City of San Diego as defined in Municipal Code section 98.0720.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply where the owner or a family member resides in the same residential building and shares a bathroom or kitchen facility with the tenant or prospective tenant (§98.0804). Acts necessary to comply with program requirements related to source of income are excepted.
rules.interaction: Defines source of income more broadly than the California FEHA definition; landlords keep the right to reject applicants for other lawful reasons consistent with federal, state and local law.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code §§ 98.0801-98.0806 (Ord. O-20986 N.S.)
rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for any person to do any of the following acts, wholly or in 
part, based on a person’s source of income  (except as may be necessary to 
comply with any program requirements related to source of income ):
rules.notes: Division added 9-18-2018 by O-20986 N.S.; effective 10-18-2018. Remedies (§98.0806) include treble one month's rent in damages for violations on or after August 1, 2019, plus injunction and fees; not used as key value.

rules.title: S.F. Rent Ordinance Section 37.10C - Prohibition on Algorithmic Rent-Setting Devices
rules.requirement: Prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices (software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents for vacant units) to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units. Tenants or the City Attorney may bring a civil action for violations.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale or use of algorithmic rent-setting devices
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential units in San Francisco; 'algorithmic device' means a device such as a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purposes of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit.
rules.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.
rules.notes: Secondary summary from the SF Rent Board news page; effective date stated in the text as October 14, 2024. The text does not give the ordinance number; citation follows the Section 37.10C reference in the Rent Ordinance (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37).

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction (S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9(a))
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for the eviction; 17 enumerated reasons are allowed, and expiration of a lease or change in ownership is not just cause.
rules.key_value: Eviction only for one of 17 enumerated just causes (Section 37.9(a))
rules.coverage_conditions: Units covered by the Rent Ordinance, including some units exempt from rent increase limits: newly constructed units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for a rent increase under Costa-Hawkins, and some tenancies where rent is regulated by another government agency. | [D082] Evictions based on owner/relative move-in, demolition/permanent removal from housing use, temporary capital improvement work or substantial rehabilitation (Ellis Act evictions have their own schedule). The rate depends on the date of service of the notice of termination of tenancy. | [D083] Applies by the date the notice of termination of tenancy was served: 3/01/26 – 2/28/27.
rules.exemptions: [D082] Temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days are governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9, not Rent Ordinance § 37.9C.
rules.interaction: Applies even to some tenancies exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limits (e.g., Costa-Hawkins-exempt units); state just cause law is not discussed in this document.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.
rules.notes: Official SF Rent Board summary page; effective date not stated in the document, so null. Relocation-assistance amounts are not covered in this document.

rules.title: San Francisco annual allowable rent increase (3/1/2026\u20132/28/2027)
rules.requirement: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6% of the tenant's base rent.
rules.key_value: 1.6% annual allowable increase (3/1/2026\u20132/28/2027)
rules.coverage_conditions: Rent-controlled units in San Francisco subject to the Rent Ordinance. | [D083] Units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance; coverage thresholds are not stated in this document.
rules.quoted_span: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
rules.notes: Announcement of the annual figure; the prior year's (3/1/2025\u20132/28/2026) figure was 1.4%. Example: $2,000 base rent x .016 = $32 increase. Citation to the Rent Ordinance is inferred; the page does not cite a section.

rules.title: Fair Chance Ordinance (affordable housing)
rules.requirement: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions. This page gives no operative details beyond that statement.
rules.key_value: Protection against use of arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions
rules.coverage_conditions: Affordable housing decisions only, per the page's description; no thresholds are stated.
rules.citation: S.F. Police Code art. 49 (Fair Chance Ordinance)
rules.quoted_span: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions.
rules.notes: Navigation or teaser text on an agency landing page. The citation comes from general knowledge, not this document. The page states no effective date, adoption date or specific requirements, so effective_date is null.

rules.title: SF security deposit interest rate
rules.requirement: Landlords must pay interest on tenant security deposits at the Rent Board rate, which is 4.2% for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
rules.key_value: 4.2% interest for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies subject to San Francisco's security deposit interest rules; thresholds are not stated in this document.
rules.quoted_span: 4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
rules.notes: Prior rates were 5.0% (3/1/25–2/28/26) and 5.2% (3/1/24–2/28/25). The citation is not given in this document and is supplied from knowledge of the SF Administrative Code.

rules.title: Santa Ana ordinance limiting algorithmic rent-setting software
rules.requirement: Landlords may not use certain algorithmic rent-setting tools, meaning software that relies on nonpublic market data, in the Santa Ana residential rental market. Tenants may sue, and need only show the prohibited software was used rather than prove active collusion.
rules.key_value: Ban on certain algorithmic rent-setting (price-fixing) software
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental housing in Santa Ana. | [D088] Residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits.
rules.exemptions: Does not restrict tools that rely on publicly available data or historical trends, or tools used for affordable housing compliance. | [D088] Pricing software relying solely on publicly available data or aggregate historical data, and tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.
rules.interaction: The newsletter says the ordinance is intended to complement broader state-level protections; no preemption issue is stated.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Municipal Code (ordinance approved by City Council March 3, 2026; ordinance number and section not stated in source)
rules.quoted_span: Bans Price-Fixing Software: Prohibits the use of certain algorithmic rent-setting tools in the local rental market.
rules.notes: Month of adoption; exact effective date not stated in source (California ordinances generally take effect after adoption, often 30 days after final passage). Secondary newsletter summary; the ordinance text, number and code section are not in this document. Civil remedies: damages, injunctive relief, up to $1,000 per violation, attorney's fees.

rules.title: Santa Ana Ordinance NS-3090 (automated rent price-fixing)
rules.requirement: Santa Ana prohibits specified anticompetitive automated rent price-fixing, and tenants may bring private claims.
rules.key_value: Ban on automated rent price-fixing
rules.coverage_conditions: [D086] Apartment owners and landlords in the City of Santa Ana; no unit-count or other thresholds stated in the article. | [D087] Residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits.
rules.exemptions: [D087] Pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data, aggregate historical data, or tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.
rules.quoted_span: Ordinance NS-3090 prohibits specified anticompetitive automated rent price-fixing; private tenant claims and up to $1,000 per violation and per month.
rules.conflict_note: Secondary source (secondary (law firm / news / mirror)); confirm against the official text.
rules.notes: Secondary source. Effective date from the table ('effective April 2, 2026'). Municipal code section not given in the document. Proposal (Santa Ana Municipal Code, algorithmic rent-setting software ordinance (ordinance number and section not stated in source), D087) adopted as Santa Ana Ordinance No. NS-3090.

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: After 30 days of tenancy, an owner may not terminate a tenancy without just cause stated in a written notice. For no-fault terminations the owner must give 3 months of relocation assistance or waive rent for the final 3 months.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 30 days; no-fault termination requires 3 months relocation assistance or 3 months rent waiver
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies generally; protection begins after the first 30 days of tenancy. | [D084] Not stated on this page.
rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; and other shared living quarters.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Municipal Code, Just Cause Eviction Ordinance (section number not stated in source)
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.
rules.notes: Secondary press release from the city; adoption date not stated (only 'Tuesday night'). At-fault causes require prior notice of the violation with a chance to cure. Owners had to notify existing tenants before December 19, 2021. Later amendments, if any, are not reflected in this document.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance
rules.requirement: Annual residential rent increases are capped at the lower of 3% or 80% of the CPI change over the most recent 12 months; no increase is allowed if CPI is negative. The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1.
rules.key_value: Lower of 3% per year or 80% of CPI change (12 months); no increase if CPI negative
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental units; the cap does not apply to residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995, or to mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990. | [D084] Not stated on this page; the page refers to the ordinance for coverage.
rules.exemptions: Owners may petition the City Manager or designee for relief from the cap by showing a larger increase is necessary for a fair and reasonable return; decision within 60 days of a complete application.

rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period.
